title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
description: How LLMs work, how to use them well and their limits: tokens, transformers, prompting, RAG and fine-tuning.

questions.prompt: What does LLM stand for?
questions.explanation: LLMs are large neural networks trained on vast amounts of text.

questions.prompt: Which neural network architecture underlies most modern LLMs?
questions.explanation: The transformer, introduced in 2017, is the basis of GPT, Claude, Llama and others.

questions.prompt: In an LLM, what is a token?
options: A chunk of text, such as a word or part of a word
questions.explanation: Text is split into tokens; models read and write token by token.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism lets each token weigh how relevant every other token is?
questions.explanation: Self-attention is the core operation of the transformer.

questions.prompt: What is a model's context window?
options: The maximum number of tokens it can consider at once
The window the chat appears in
The time a request may take
The size of its training set
questions.explanation: Prompt plus response must fit within the context window.

questions.prompt: Raising the sampling temperature generally makes output...
questions.explanation: Higher temperature flattens the probability distribution over next tokens.

questions.prompt: What does RAG stand for?
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant documents and gives them to the model as context.

questions.prompt: In LLMs, a hallucination is...
options: Confidently stated information that is false or made up
An image generated by the model
questions.explanation: Models can produce fluent but wrong statements, so important facts need checking.

questions.prompt: Which practices help reduce hallucinations?
options: Asking the model to cite its sources
questions.explanation: Grounding, citations and verification help; a higher temperature tends to add randomness.

questions.prompt: Which are common ways to adapt an LLM to a specific task?
questions.explanation: Better prompts, extra training and supplying context are the main levers.

questions.prompt: Which are real risks when building LLM applications?
questions.explanation: Untrusted input, data exposure and wrong answers all need safeguards.

questions.prompt: LLMs generate text one token at a time.
questions.explanation: They are autoregressive: each new token depends on the ones before it.

questions.prompt: An LLM automatically knows about events after its training data was collected.
questions.explanation: Without tools or retrieval, a model only knows what was in its training data.

questions.prompt: Embeddings represent text as vectors of numbers.
questions.explanation: Similar meanings end up close together, which powers semantic search.

questions.prompt: Pre-training teaches a model to predict the next ___ in large amounts of text.
questions.explanation: Next-token prediction is the core pre-training objective.

questions.prompt: Further training a pre-trained model on a smaller task-specific dataset is called ___.
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning adjusts the model's weights for a narrower task.

questions.prompt: A model has an 8,000-token context window and the prompt uses 6,500 tokens. How many tokens are left for the response?
Put the steps of a RAG pipeline in order.
items: Retrieve the chunks most similar to the question
Generate an answer using the retrieved chunks
questions.explanation: Index first (chunk + embed), then retrieve at question time and generate.

questions.prompt: Order the typical stages of training a chat assistant.
items: Pre-training on a large text corpus
questions.explanation: Broad knowledge first, then instruction following, then preference tuning.

questions.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.

pairs.right: The input text given to the model
Controls how random the output is
The unit of text a model reads and writes

questions.explanation: These four terms come up in almost every LLM discussion.
